title: AWS Config Rule Compliance Drift

controlTest.positiveScenario: Inject sample events matching UC-4.1.66 SPL; confirm the search returns rows and alert fires.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Replay benign traffic without matching markers; confirm UC-4.1.66 search returns zero rows.

dataSources: `index=aws` sourcetype=`aws:config:notification` collected via `Splunk_TA_aws`; validate ingest with `| stats count by sourcetype`.
spl:
index=aws sourcetype="aws:config:notification" configRuleList{}.complianceType=*
| table _time userIdentity.arn eventName sourceIPAddress
| eval uc_marker="UC-4.1.66_aws_config_rule_complian_66"
| sort -_time
description: Resources oscillating between COMPLIANT and NON_COMPLIANT indicate automation fights or manual changes—drift trends surface systemic issues.
value: Detecting aws config rule compliance drift early reduces mean time to contain cloud incidents, supports audit logging controls, and prevents silent misconfiguration drift across accounts.
implementation: Ingest configuration item change streams. Track flapping rules weekly. Alert when critical rules (encryption, public access) change state more than N times per day. Root-cause with CloudTrail correlation.
visualization: Table (resource, rule, changes), Line chart (compliant % over time), Single value (flapping resources).
cimSpl:
| tstats `summariesonly` max(Performance.cpu_load_percent) as peak
  from datamodel=Performance.All_Performance
  by Performance.object Performance.host span=1h
| where isnotnull(peak)
| sort - peak
dataModelAcceleration: Performance: enable if `aws:cloudwatch` (or your metric store) is mapped to CIM Performance, or use `mstats` on the same CloudWatch metrics. Enable Data Model Acceleration for the CIM data models in `cimModels` once `Splunk_TA_aws` (and any CIM tags/aliases) map your fields; otherwise the `cimSpl` summary search may be empty. Step 2 on raw or metric indexes stays primary for most sites.
knownFalsePositives: Planned deploys, game-day tests, and vendor maintenance that you expect to move CPU, error, or lag metrics; compare with the change window.
detailedImplementation:
Prerequisites
• Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud with search access to `index=aws`.
• Install and configure `Splunk_TA_aws` with the modular input for `aws:config:notification`.
• Prerequisite crawl UC(s): UC-4.1.78.
• Confirm field extractions in `props.conf` for `userIdentity.arn` and related actor fields.

Step 1 — Configure data collection
Ingest configuration item change streams. Track flapping rules weekly. Alert when critical rules (encryption, public access) change state more than N times per day. Root-cause with CloudTrail correlation.
Validate ingest before alerting:
```spl
index=aws sourcetype="aws:config:notification" | stats count by sourcetype
```

Step 2 — Create the search and alert
```spl
index=aws sourcetype="aws:config:notification" configRuleList{}.complianceType=*
| table _time userIdentity.arn eventName sourceIPAddress
| eval uc_marker="UC-4.1.66_aws_config_rule_complian_66"
| sort -_time
```

Understanding this SPL
Scopes `aws:config:notification` in `index=aws` to detect aws config rule compliance drift. Tune thresholds to your change cadence; exclude break-glass principals and sandbox accounts via a lookup.

Step 3 — Validate
Compare to the provider cloud console audit view for the same 24-hour window. Confirm row counts and `userIdentity.arn` values match the vendor console. Run `| fieldsummary` on a 1-hour sample to verify extractions.

Step 4 — Operationalize and troubleshoot
Save as `4_1_66_alert` with severity aligned to `medium` criticality. Dashboard: Table (resource, rule, changes), Line chart (compliant % over time), Single value (flapping resources)..
Failure modes: (1) no events — verify modular input/API credentials and index routing; (2) empty actor fields — upgrade `Splunk_TA_aws` and review alias mappings; (3) API throttling — reduce poll frequency or enable queue buffering; (4) alert fatigue — tune thresholds and document exclusions in knownFalsePositives.
grandmaExplanation: We watch cloud logs for signs of aws config rule compliance drift so your team catches problems in your online services before customers or auditors do.
